monitored_text: Resources / Machining Design / Wire Harness: Components, Types, and Manufacturing Wire Harness: Components, Types, and Manufacturing Written by Megan Conniff Updated by Audrius Zidonis PhD 13 min read Published November 26, 2026 A wire harness is an organized bundle of wires, terminals, connectors that carries power, signals through a vehicle or machine. A wire harness replaces loose point to point wiring in cars, trucks, aircraft, appliances, factory equipment. Copper conductors in American Wire Gauge (AWG) sizes from 22 to 10 carry current, whereas insulation, sleeving, tape protect the bundle. Terminals crimped onto wire ends lock into connector housings, completing each circuit. Vehicle makers, aerospace contractors, machine builders specify harnesses to a drawing, then verify each build by electrical testing. Components include wires, terminals, connectors, protective coverings, mounting hardware. Types range from engine, chassis, body harnesses to industrial, aerospace, military assemblies. Engineering considerations cover electrical load, routing path, operating environment, connector selection. Manufacturing runs from wire cutting, stripping through crimping, assembly on a harness board, continuity testing. Custom manufacturing supplies the supporting parts, including computer numerical control (CNC) machined pins, injection molded housings, 3D printed prototypes, sheet metal brackets. Pull testing, insulation resistance testing catch crimp, pinout errors before installation. What Is a Wire Harness? A wire harness is an assembly that groups wires, cables into one organized unit. Harnesses replace loose wiring (easier installation, protection from vibration, abrasion, simpler troubleshooting). Modern passenger vehicles carry over 1 km (0.6 mi) of wiring, so one harness routed in a single pass replaces hundreds of loose runs. Color coding, printed wire numbers, labeled branches let technicians trace a circuit quickly during repairs. Sleeving, tape, clips shield the bundle from engine vibration, rubbing against sheet metal edges. What Is a Wiring Harness in a Car? A wiring harness in a car is an assembly that routes power, signals among the battery, engine, sensors, lighting, controls. The assembly replaces point to point wiring, so one trunk line carrying branches reaches each component. Passenger cars run 12 volt systems, whereas electric vehicles add 400 volt or 800 volt high voltage cables in orange sheathing. Branches split off the main trunk toward the dashboard, doors, headlights, rear lamps, fuel pump. What Is the Difference Between a Wire Harness and a Cable Harness? A wire harness differs from a cable harness in construction. A wire harness bundles insulated wires, whereas a cable harness groups cables inside a shared outer jacket. Automotive, appliance, control panel wiring uses wire harnesses, held together by tape, loom, ties. Cable harnesses route Ethernet, coaxial, shielded multi conductor cables in medical devices, robots, test equipment. The outer jacket of a cable harness protects the cables from abrasion, moisture, electromagnetic interference. Is a Wiring Loom the Same as a Wire Harness? Yes, a wiring loom equals a wire harness in British usage, since the term names the complete assembly. American shops call protective sleeving loom, including split corrugated tubing in polyethylene or nylon. Parts catalogs in Australia, Ireland follow the British meaning. Purchase orders avoid confusion by naming the item, either a harness assembly or loom tubing, and the drawing number. The terms overlap, but tubing protects a harness, whereas the harness carries the circuits. What Are the Components of a Wire Harness? The components of a wire harness are wires, terminals, connectors, protective coverings, mounting hardware. Wires carry current, terminals crimped onto wire ends make the electrical joint. Connector housings hold terminals in fixed positions, so a mating connector completes each circuit in one push. Tape, sleeving, conduit protect the bundle, whereas clips, grommets, cable ties, brackets secure the routing. Weak crimps, cracked insulation, missing clips cause field failures, so component quality sets harness reliability. What Materials Are Used in a Wiring Harness? A wiring harness uses copper conductors, polymer insulation, and braided or corrugated sleeving. Insulation options include polyvinyl chloride (PVC) rated near 105 °C (221°F), cross-linked polyethylene (XLPE) rated near 125 °C (257 °F), and silicone rated near 200 °C (392 °F). Heat near engines favors XLPE and silicone, whereas oil, fuel, and coolant demand chemical-resistant jackets. Repeated flexing in robots and door hinges demands stranded copper, since solid copper cracks. Braided sleeving protects against abrasion, corrugated sleeving adds crush resistance. What Are the Connectors and Terminals in a Wire Harness Made of? Terminals and connector contacts in a wire harness are made of brass or plated copper alloys. Tin plating protects standard contacts, whereas gold plating of about 0.76 µm (30 microinches) protects low-voltage signal contacts. Precision metal parts (pins, sockets, connector shells) come from computer numerical control (CNC) turning, milling, holding diameters near ±0.05 mm (±0.002 in). Tight tolerances, plating thickness controls decide fit, current rating, corrosion life of parts produced through CNC machining . How Are Wire Harness Connector Housings Made? Wire harness connector housings are made by injection molding, which injects molten plastic into a steel mold. Volume runs justify tooling, since cycles last 15 to 45 seconds. Nylon 66 offers toughness, whereas polybutylene terephthalate (PBT) offers dimensional stability, low moisture uptake. Flame retardant grades meet Underwriters Laboratories (UL) 94 V-0, which requires flaming to stop within 10 seconds after each flame application. Locking tabs, terminal cavities, keying ribs mold into the housing in a single shot. Can 3D Printing Be Used to Prototype Wire Harness Components? Yes, 3D printing is used to prototype wire harness components before tooling is committed. Printers produce connector housings, cable clips, routing fixtures in nylon, photopolymer resin. Layer thickness of 0.1 mm to 0.3 mm (0.004 in to 0.012 in) sets surface finish. Test fits in vehicles, machines confirm clearances within days. Printed parts show lower strength, lower heat resistance than molded nylon, PBT, so final production uses injection molding. Prototype housings, clips, fixtures are produced through 3D printing . What are the types of wiring harness? Types of wiring harness include engine, chassis, body, industrial, aerospace or military assemblies. Construction, protection requirements differ by operating environment, from a 12 volt passenger car circuit to a 28 volt aircraft system exposed to altitude, temperature swings. Heat, vibration, moisture, chemicals, flexing cycles decide the insulation, sleeving, connector choices, whereas drawings, standards fix the build requirements. The types of wiring harness are listed below. Engine Wiring Harness: An engine wiring harness links the engine control unit (ECU), injectors, ignition coils, sensors. Cables run in zones reaching 125 °C (257 °F), so XLPE insulation, heat resistant sleeving protect the circuits. Oil resistant jackets, sealed connectors block fuel, coolant, moisture. The starter circuit draws 150 A to 400 A during cranking, so fusible links, relay connections protect the circuits from overload. The harness carries crank, cam, oxygen sensor signals. Chassis Wiring Harness: A chassis wiring harness runs along the vehicle frame to the brakes, suspension sensors, fuel pump, rear lighting. Anti lock braking system (ABS) wheel speed sensors send signals through the harness at each wheel. Underbody routing exposes the harness to water, road salt, gravel, so sealed connectors, abrasion resistant sleeving protect the circuits. Clips space the harness 25 mm (1 in) from exhaust components. Rubber grommets seal each pass through body panels. Body Wiring Harness: A body wiring harness serves the cabin, linking the dashboard, door modules, seats, interior lighting, infotainment, climate controls. Door harnesses flex each time a door opens, so stranded copper, flexible jackets resist fatigue over the life of the door hinge. Body control modules switch windows, locks, mirrors, wipers through the harness. Branch lengths vary from 100 mm (4 in) to 3 m (118 in), depending on the vehicle size. Industrial Wire Harness: An industrial wire harness connects motors, sensors, drives, control panels in machinery, robots, conveyors, packaging lines. Voltages reach 600 V in standard machinery cable, so insulation ratings, cable shielding follow UL rules. Oil resistant, flame retardant jackets resist coolant, cutting fluid in machine tools. Continuous flex cables rated to millions of bend cycles move inside robot arms, drag chains. Terminal blocks, circular connectors (M12, M23) speed field replacement. Aerospace or Military Wire Harness: An aerospace or military wire harness links avionics, flight controls, sensors, actuators through lightweight, high reliability assemblies. Wire insulated in polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE), polyimide resists temperatures from −65 °C to 200 °C (−85 °F to 392 °F). Builders follow Class 3 of the Association Connecting Electronics Industries (IPC), Wire Harness Manufacturers Association (WHMA) standard IPC/WHMA-A-620, which governs high reliability assemblies. Shielded twisted pair cables block electromagnetic interference near radar, radio equipment. What Does an Engine Wiring Harness Do? An engine wiring harness connects the ECU, injectors, ignition, sensors. The ECU reads crankshaft position, coolant temperature, oxygen sensor signals, then holds each injector open from one to 10 milliseconds. Heat resistance matters, since underhood temperatures reach 125 °C (257 °F) in engine bays. Cross linked jackets, sealed connectors block engine oil, coolant, fuel vapor. Heat shield sleeves, spiral wrap protect branches near turbochargers, which exceed 700 °C (1,292 °F). What Is the Difference Between a Custom Wiring Harness and an Aftermarket Wiring Harness? A custom wiring harness differs from an aftermarket wiring harness in specification. A custom harness is built to a specific drawing, whereas an aftermarket harness is a ready made replacement or universal kit. Custom harnesses match lengths, branch points, connectors to the machine, whereas universal kits need trimming, splicing. Aftermarket kits cost less per unit, whereas custom builds spread tooling, setup costs across the order. Stocked kits ship in days, whereas custom harnesses take two to six weeks. Are Industrial Wire Harnesses Built Differently From Automotive Ones? Yes, industrial wire harnesses are built differently from automotive ones in voltage, environmental sealing, flexing cycles, compliance standards. Automotive harnesses run on 12 volt or 48 volt systems, whereas industrial harnesses carry 24 volt control signals, 480 volt motor power. Robot harnesses survive millions of flex cycles, whereas a car door harness sees tens of thousands. Standards differ (UL 508A covers control panels, International Organization for Standardization (ISO) 6722 covers road vehicle cables). How Is a Wire Harness Designed? Engineers lay out a wire harness from four inputs (electrical load, routing path, operating environment, connector selection). Electrical load sets wire gauge, from 18 AWG at 10 A to 12 AWG at 25 A. Routing paths set branch lengths, bend radii of at least four times the cable diameter, clip spacing. Environment, connector selection set insulation, sealing, terminal families, which determine tooling, crimp tools. Standard terminals, fewer branches lower cost, since each unique part adds inventory, crimp setups. What Does a Wire Harness Drawing Include? A wire harness drawing includes wire gauges, colors, lengths, pin assignments, connector part numbers, branch layout. A wire list names each wire (W12, 18 AWG, red, 1,250 mm (49.2 in)). Pin tables map each terminal to a connector cavity, so assemblers insert wire W12 into cavity A3. Branch layout shows breakout points, dimensions measured in millimeters, tolerances near ±10 mm (±0.4 in). The drawing gives builders, inspectors the build instructions, test limits, revision history. How Do Sheet Metal Brackets and Enclosures Protect a Wire Harness? Sheet metal brackets, junction boxes, guards protect a wire harness by holding routing in place, shielding the bundle from heat, abrasion. Brackets fix clip positions, so a harness stays 25 mm (1 in) clear of exhaust parts. Junction boxes house splices, relays, fuses inside sealed aluminum or steel enclosures. Laser cutting, bending, forming produce the parts from sheets of 0.8 mm to 3 mm (0.03 in to 0.12 in) thickness. Prototype, production runs include sheet metal brackets and enclosures . How Is a Wire Harness Manufactured? A wire harness is manufactured through a flow from wire cutting, stripping to crimping, assembly, testing. Machines cut wire to length within ±1 mm, strip 3 mm to 8 mm (0.12 in to 0.31 in) of insulation, crimp terminals. Workers then route wires on a harness board, a full size print of the drawing that holds connectors, branches in position. Production is largely manual, since flexible, branching bundles resist full automation. What Are the Steps in Cable Harness Assembly? The steps in cable harness assembly run from wire cutting, stripping to continuity testing. First, machines cut wire to length, strip 6 mm (0.24 in) of insulation. Second, crimp tools press terminals onto the conductors. Third, assemblers insert terminals into connector housings until locking tabs click. Fourth, workers bundle wires on the harness board, following the branch layout. Fifth, tape, sleeving cover the bundle. Lastly, testers run continuity checks, confirming each circuit matches the pin table. How Does a Prototype Wire Harness Differ From a Production Harness? A prototype wire harness differs from a production harness in purpose, since prototype builds validate fit, routing in small quantities. Teams build one to 10 samples, then adjust the drawing after test fits. Rapid prototyping of surrounding parts (brackets, housings, fixtures) runs in parallel, so clearances get checked early. Production harnesses follow a frozen drawing, released tooling, standard crimp, test processes. Prototype lead time runs days, whereas production tooling, process validation take weeks. Can a Wire Harness Be Fully Automated? No, a wire harness is not fully automated. Machines automate cutting, stripping, crimping, reaching 1,000 wires per hour. Final routing, assembly stay largely manual, since branching, flexible bundles resist robotic handling. Connector insertion, taping, sleeving, harness board layout need hand dexterity, vision checks, so assemblers perform the steps. Complex vehicle harnesses hold hundreds of circuits, so full automation stays out of reach. Research cells test robotic routing, yet production lines keep manual boards. How Do You Choose a Wire Harness Manufacturer? Buyers choose a wire harness manufacturer by checking quality certifications, testing capability, prototyping support, lead time, volume capacity. Certifications (ISO 9001, International Automotive Task Force (IATF) 16949, IPC/WHMA-A-620) show a documented quality system. Testing capability covers continuity, insulation resistance, pull testing on each shipped unit. Prototyping support shortens development, since a supplier that builds samples in days, then scales to volume, avoids a second qualification. Lead time, annual volume capacity, quoted tolerances decide the match to the program. What Certifications Should Wire Harness Manufacturers Have? Wire harness manufacturers hold IPC/WHMA-A-620, ISO 9001, IATF 16949 certifications, depending on the industry served. IPC/WHMA-A-620 sets workmanship criteria in three classes, covering crimps, soldering, routing, whereas Class 3 covers high reliability products. ISO 9001 signals a documented quality management system, audited by a third party. IATF 16949 signals automotive process control, including traceability, failure analysis, corrective action. Aerospace work adds AS9100, medical work adds ISO 13485. ISO certificates run on a three year cycle, followed by yearly surveillance audits. How Do You Test a Wiring Harness Before Installation? Technicians test a wiring harness before installation through continuity, insulation resistance, pull testing. Continuity testing checks that each pin connects to the correct pin, using a test board that reads open, short, miswired circuits. Insulation resistance testing applies 500 volts direct current, expecting readings above 100 megohms. Pull testing loads crimped terminals to a set force, about 36 N (8 lbf) on 20 AWG wire. Tests catch crimp, pinout errors early, which prevents field failures after installation. Disclaimer The content appearing on this webpage is for informational purposes only. text_excerpt: Resources / Machining Design / Wire Harness: Components, Types, and Manufacturing Wire Harness: Components, Types, and Manufacturing Written by Megan Conniff Updated by Audrius Zidonis PhD 13 min read Published November 26, 2026 A wire harness is an organized bundle of wires, terminals, connectors that carries power, signals through a vehicle or machine. A wire harness replaces loose point to point wiring in cars, trucks, aircraft, appliances, factory equipment. Copper conductors in American Wire Gauge (AWG) sizes from 22 to 10 carry current, whereas insulation, sleeving, tape protect the bundle. Terminals crimped onto wire ends lock into connector housings, completing each circuit. Vehicle makers, aerospace contractors, machine builders specify harnesses to a drawing, then verify each build by electrical testing. Components include wires, terminals, connectors, protective coverings, mounting hardware. Types range from engine, chassis, body harnesses to industrial, aerospace, military assemblies.
